claims.text: The NbMoCrTiAl composite can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering produces an NbMoCrTiAl composite containing in-situ TiC and Al2O3 phases.
The processed composite contains approximately 32 vol.% TiC and 7 vol.% Al2O3.
The as-cast NbMoCrTiAl alloy has a homogeneous BCC matrix.
The TiC and Al2O3 particles are uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix.
The in-situ ceramic particles refine the matrix grains.
The in-situ ceramic particles impede dislocation motion.
The dispersed ceramic particles enhance oxidation resistance.
Second-phase strengthening and grain refinement caused by the ceramic phases increase compressive strength.
Al2O3 contributes to a protective, low-permeability oxide film that limits oxygen ingress.
The alloying elements in the composite have lower activation than conventional refractory metals and therefore reduce long-lived radioactive products.
Under high-temperature and irradiation-simulated conditions, the composite will have roughly 50% greater compressive strength than the as-cast alloy.
The processed composite will exhibit improved oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast alloy.
The processed composite will exhibit reduced activation relative to conventional refractory materials.
The as-cast NbMoCrTiAl alloy has lower compressive strength than the processed composite.
The as-cast alloy lacks the beneficial TiC-Al2O3 composite microstructure.
Room-temperature compression testing showed a composite fracture strength of 1542 MPa, approximately 50% above the as-cast value of 1010 MPa.
Oxidation studies show that the composite is promising.
The composite's activation under a full fusion neutron spectrum and long-term irradiation has not been fully quantified.
Many conventional high-activation refractory metals present persistent-radioactivity problems.
